name: Cursor Cloud Agents
description: Cursor's server-side agent product (formerly Background Agents), distinct from the local IDE. Each task runs in an isolated cloud Linux VM with a fresh ephemeral checkout of the repo, executes asynchronously, and produces merge-ready PRs. Sessions can be handed off cloud<->local with state and history preserved. Triggerable from web/IDE/Slack/GitHub/Linear/mobile/automations, scalable to many parallel agents, and self-hostable via a Helm chart / Kubernetes operator using a WorkerDeployment resource.

identity_and_auth.user_identity_model: Same account model as the Cursor ecosystem: email+password, GitHub OAuth, Google OAuth, magic link, and SAML 2.0 SSO (Teams/Enterprise) via OAuth 2.0, with SCIM provisioning on Enterprise. Cloud agents additionally require connecting a git provider (GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, or Bitbucket Cloud) so the VM can clone the repo. An authenticated, subscription-bearing account is required (Pro $20/mo and above). Triggers from Slack/GitHub/Linear are bound to the connected account/installation.
identity_and_auth.multi_user_collaboration: Team/org first-class. Teams and Enterprise plans add SAML SSO, SCIM, admin dashboards, Privacy Mode enforcement, and team/enterprise-managed hooks. Agents and their status are surfaced in a shared/unified Agents window; teams coordinate via the connected git provider (PRs) and Slack threads. Parallelism limits are per-user and per-team (e.g. up to 10 workers per user, 50 per team on self-hosted pools, larger on request). Self-hosted deployments inherit org RBAC at the Kubernetes layer.

workspace_model.workspace_definition: A workspace is anchored to a connected git repository (or a multi-repo set). Each cloud agent task gets a fresh VM that clones the repo at the current HEAD of a specified base branch; the agent then works on its own branch. Multi-repo environments let a single configured dev environment contain all repos an agent needs (read/write/test across them in one session). The 'workspace' is therefore repo-centric and realized as an ephemeral VM filesystem per task, not a long-lived directory on the user's machine.
workspace_model.workspace_session_binding: Each Cloud Agent session claims one worker/VM at a time and works on its own branch, so a session is bound to a task + branch + ephemeral VM. Multiple sessions can run concurrently against the same workspace/repo (parallel agents, each in its own VM/branch), isolated from each other. Sessions appear in the unified Agents window across surfaces (web, mobile, Slack, GitHub, desktop). A session is resumable via a chat/session id and can be continued with follow-up messages, or moved between cloud and local.
workspace_model.context_scoping: Workspace/repo-level: .cursor/environment.json (committed, defines the dev environment), .cursor/rules/*.mdc and AGENTS.md (committed instructions), .cursor/hooks.json (project hooks; team + enterprise hooks on Enterprise), and MCP configurations. Secrets are scoped via the Secrets tab (recommended) or pulled from the local/cluster environment in self-hosted mode (never sent back to Cursor's orchestration plane). Session-level: the task prompt, queued follow-ups, attached context, and the Slack/GitHub thread the agent reads before starting. Global account-level: User Rules and connected integrations.
workspace_model.config_file_instruction_precedence: Inherits the same rules cascade as local Cursor (Team Rules -> Project Rules -> User Rules; nested AGENTS.md combine with parents, deeper/more specific taking precedence; .mdc must be flat in .cursor/rules/). Cloud-specific config adds .cursor/environment.json (environment setup: install/update command, snapshot, or Dockerfile) and .cursor/hooks.json (executed by the worker). environment.json is meant to be committed so every agent and teammate inherits an identical box. [uncertain]
workspace_model.source_corpus_grounding_scope: Not a bounded-source research product. Grounding is the cloned repo(s) inside the VM plus any MCP tools/integrations and the triggering thread (e.g. the full Slack thread is read for context before work begins). Multi-repo support broadens the grounding set to several repositories within one session.

persistence_and_history.persistence_mechanism: Decoupled, server-side. Cursor explicitly separates three components: the agent loop, machine (VM) state, and conversation state. The agent loop runs in Temporal (a durable workflow engine) rather than on the VM, so pod/VM lifecycles are managed independently. Conversation state uses a dedicated append-only storage + streaming layer that streams updates to web/desktop clients and handles retries (clients can rewind the stream on a retried step). The Cursor SDK exposes pluggable agent/run metadata stores -- SQLite (default), an append-only JSONL store (readable/diffable/checkin-able), or a custom LocalAgentStore (e.g. Postgres) -- for resuming agents after process restart. Machine state is captured as reusable snapshots (see snapshot_state_restore).
persistence_and_history.session_history: Conversation history is persisted server-side via the append-only conversation layer and is browsable in the unified Agents window (web/mobile/IDE/Slack). Sessions are addressable by a chat/session id, enabling resume (cursor-agent --resume <chatId>) and follow-up messages that continue the same session (e.g. to fix CI failures). The SDK's JSONL store option yields a plain append-only file that can be read, diffed, and version-controlled; SQLite and Postgres backends are also supported. Agents produce durable artifacts (PRs, screenshots, videos, logs) attached to the session for review. Export/portability beyond the JSONL store and git PRs is not strongly documented. [uncertain]
persistence_and_history.memory_layering: Durable instruction layers come from committed rules/AGENTS.md and (project-scoped) auto-generated Memories, same as local. Cloud adds machine-state snapshots as a separate durable layer (environment, not conversation). Ephemeral thread state (the live run, VM working tree) is distinct from the durable conversation store and from the snapshot store. Event-driven/automated agents can optionally remember outcomes of previous runs to improve over time, a lightweight cross-run memory. The three-way decoupling (agent loop / machine state / conversation state) is the architectural expression of this layering.
persistence_and_history.search_retrieval_history: Sessions across surfaces are aggregated in the unified Agents window and addressable by id for resume/reference. There is no prominently documented full-text or semantic search across all past cloud sessions; retrieval is primarily list/sidebar browsing plus id-based resume, with automations optionally recalling prior run outcomes. [uncertain]
persistence_and_history.lifecycle_ttl_cleanup: VM/machine state is ephemeral per task: each task gets a fresh VM, and filesystem changes/dependencies/artifacts are scoped to that VM only; uncommitted work that isn't pushed to a branch/PR is effectively discarded when the VM is torn down. In self-hosted pools, --idle-release-timeout keeps a worker alive briefly after a session ends for follow-up messages, then the pod exits (code 0) and is replaced. Conversation state persists in the durable append-only/Temporal-backed store independent of VM teardown, so history outlives the VM. Snapshots persist as reusable base environments and can be updated (incl. an undocumented agentCanUpdateSnapshot flag) when the dependency tree changes.

execution_and_isolation.sandbox_isolation_model: Strong VM-level isolation. Each task runs in its own isolated Linux VM (background agents run in Docker containers on AWS VMs) with a full dev environment: own filesystem/disk, terminal sessions, network stack, package manager, browser, and a running app instance. The repo is cloned fresh (ephemeral checkout) per task; the user's laptop is not involved and there is no resource competition between agents or with the user. Network access is available for setup/runtime (clone, install, reach APIs). In self-hosted mode, tool execution and code stay entirely within the customer's network; only outbound HTTPS to Cursor's cloud for orchestration/model/UX is required (no inbound ports, no VPN), and secrets never leave the customer's plane.
execution_and_isolation.snapshot_state_restore: First-class. The environment (installed packages, system deps, optionally .env.local) is captured in a reusable snapshot so future agents boot faster and can immediately run/test the software. Configured via .cursor/environment.json (agent-led setup, a saved snapshot, or a Dockerfile). Boot flow: start from base -> run idempotent update/install command -> if it took more than a few seconds, Cursor takes an internal checkpoint snapshot and starts future agents from it (incremental work on dependency changes). Snapshots are independent of conversation history (machine state vs conversation state are decoupled) and can be auto-updated when the dependency tree changes (undocumented agentCanUpdateSnapshot flag).
execution_and_isolation.cloud_local_handoff: Yes -- bidirectional with state+history preserved. A local session can be pushed to the cloud (prefix a message with &, or /in-cloud to spin a cloud subagent on its own VM/branch); a cloud session can be pulled into the local IDE with all modified files and context intact to finish manually. Sessions are also portable across web, mobile, Slack, GitHub, and desktop via the unified Agents window. Self-hosting is supported (see implementation_stack).
execution_and_isolation.parallelism_subagent_fanout: Massively parallel. Many agents can run simultaneously, each in its own VM/branch (e.g. 10 features in 10 VMs), with no contention on local resources. Individual paid users can run up to 10 parallel subagents per session; team accounts support up to 50 parallel workers; self-hosted pools document up to 10 workers per user and 50 per team, with higher limits on request. Worktrees (Cursor 3.2) let agents run isolated tasks across branches and merge back. Each Cloud Agent session claims one worker at a time; the Kubernetes operator scales the worker pool to the task queue.
execution_and_isolation.trigger_surface: Broad: web (cursor.com/agents), the desktop IDE/Agents window, mobile (PWA), Slack (@Cursor in a thread; reads the whole thread for context), GitHub, GitLab, Linear, and Automations (schedule- or event-driven via GitHub/GitLab/Slack/webhooks, with MCP tools). Automations can run unattended on a cron/event and optionally post results to Slack or comment on PRs.

implementation.implementation_stack: Orchestration uses Temporal for the durable agent loop, decoupled from the VM so pod lifecycles are independent (an evolution away from the early fragile work-stealing design). Execution runs in isolated Linux VMs -- background agents in Docker containers on AWS VMs -- with ephemeral repo clones from GitHub/GitLab/Azure DevOps/Bitbucket. Conversation state uses a bespoke append-only storage + streaming layer with retry/rewind semantics; SDK persistence stores are pluggable (SQLite default, append-only JSONL, or custom LocalAgentStore such as Postgres). Environments are defined by .cursor/environment.json with reusable snapshots and internal checkpointing of the install step. Self-hosting: a Helm chart + Kubernetes operator where you declare a WorkerDeployment resource (pool size); the controller handles scaling, rolling updates, and lifecycle, watching WorkerDeployment across namespaces with cluster-wide RBAC. Workers start with --pool, --idle-release-timeout, and a controller-managed token file; secrets are pulled from cluster/.env sources and never sent to Cursor. A fleet-management API supports autoscaling on non-Kubernetes infra (e.g. Render). Project/team/enterprise hooks run from .cursor/hooks.json on the worker.
implementation.applicability_to_labmate: Cursor Cloud Agents validate several Labmate design choices and add useful refinements. (1) Decouple the three concerns Cursor names -- agent loop, machine/active state, and conversation state -- which maps directly to Labmate's split: LangGraph thread_id checkpointing for the agent loop, Redis Streams (TTL) for active/ephemeral session state (analogous to Cursor's ephemeral VM + idle-release-timeout), and MongoDB long-term session docs for durable conversation history (analogous to Cursor's append-only conversation store that outlives the VM). (2) Make conversation history append-only and streamable with retry/rewind semantics -- a strong pattern for Labmate's Discord connector, where partial outputs may need to be superseded on retry. (3) Use a stable session/chat id as the resume handle (cursor-agent --resume <chatId>); Labmate should mint a workspace_id + session_id and support id-based resume + queued follow-up messages rather than re-deriving state. (4) Treat environment/machine snapshots as a layer separate from history if Labmate ever runs sandboxed tool execution -- cache idempotent setup and checkpoint it (Cursor's install-then-snapshot flow). (5) For the Discord connector as a session entry point, mirror Cursor's multi-surface trigger model: one durable session addressable from many surfaces, with the triggering thread read for context. (6) The self-hosted WorkerDeployment / pool-with-idle-timeout model is a concrete reference if Labmate later needs sandboxed parallel agents with TTL-bounded worker lifecycles.
